title: Dust and worlds (section 30)
hook: a world ground into dust: are the specks many? the world is not a world, so called

segments.voice: Yesterday, neither coming nor going: the Tathagata goes nowhere and comes from nowhere, and that's why he has the name. Your line: neither coming nor going.

Late afternoon, and the light comes sideways through a kitchen window. Suddenly the air, which looked empty, is full. Specks drift, turn, flare and vanish. They were there the whole time; the light just caught them. A child on a beach makes the same discovery in reverse. She builds a castle, proud of every tower, and an hour later the tide makes it sand again. Which one was it really? Section thirty of the Diamond Sutra blows that question up to the size of a world.
screen: `SIDEWAYS LIGHT, FULL AIR.` → `A CASTLE BECOMES SAND.` → `WHICH ONE WAS IT?`

segments.voice: The Buddha asks Subhuti, in paraphrase: suppose someone ground a whole vast world system down to dust, finer and finer. Would that heap of specks be many? Many indeed, Subhuti says. Then his reason, and it's a strange one. If the heap were a real thing in itself, the Buddha would not have called it a heap. What's taught as a heap of specks is taught as no heap, and that's why it's called a heap of specks. He turns the same blade on the world. The world system the Tathagata speaks of is not a world system; that's why it's called a world. Why say this? Because if a world really existed as one solid thing, Subhuti says, that would be a grasping at a lump: taking a heap of parts as one fixed whole. The Buddha answers that this grasping at a lump can't truly be put into words. It isn't a thing. Yet ordinary people get hold of it anyway. The mind is a lump-maker. My whole life. This entire mess. Everything is falling apart. Each feels like one solid block. Section thirty grinds the block gently into specks, and then won't let you make the specks into solid little blocks either. Neither the world nor the dust is the final, fixed thing. What's left is closer to that kitchen air: full, moving, and lit.
screen: `A WORLD GROUND TO DUST.` · `A HEAP IS CALLED A HEAP.` · `GRASPING AT A LUMP.` · `THE MIND IS A LUMP-MAKER.` · then, large: `A WORLD OF DUST.`

segments.voice: If there's a window with sun nearby, find the angle where the air shows its specks and watch them drift; if not, close your eyes and let the mind's own pictures drift the same way. Hold one thing that feels like a solid lump today, a worry, a task, a judgment of yourself. See it as specks, a few moments, thoughts and sensations moving in the light, and let it stay loose.
Dust and worlds. Section thirty: a world ground into dust; the heap of specks is no heap, and the world no world, and so they're called heap and world. Today's word.
Your line: a world of dust. A heap is only called a heap. Day one thousand one hundred forty-seven, done.

howItsDone: Students of the Diamond Sutra in Mahayana communities read section 30 as a lesson in how the mind makes solid wholes out of parts; it's chanted with the rest of the sutra and taken up in study and meditation.

chat.says: If the world is 'no world, so called a world,' is the Diamond Sutra saying it's fake?
options: No. It says the world isn't one solid lump, and even its specks aren't fixed things.
Yes. The sutra says nothing appears at all, so there's no world and no dust.
It means the world is one solid whole that can never be broken into parts.
chat.meaning: Section thirty cuts the grasping at a lump: a world isn't one fixed whole, and its dust isn't fixed either. So called, not fake.

notes: Section 30 paraphrased, not quoted from Max Müller (wording unverified): check the world system ground to dust, Subhuti's 'many indeed' and his reason, 'world system is no system, so called', and 'grasping at a lump' (pinda-graha) as inexpressible yet held by ordinary people.
The sutra's scale (a 'great thousand' world system) is left as 'a whole vast world system' under the claims rule.
The kitchen-air and sandcastle images are the writer's illustrations, not the sutra's.
